topic.title: Solving simple trigonometric equations in a given range
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. A trigonometric equation follows the graph question near the front of every paper read: Summer 2018 Q3(b) (5 marks, a bracket), Summer 2019 Q4(b), Summer 2022 Q4(b) (3 marks then 3), Summer 2023 Q3(b) (3 marks then 3), Summer 2024 Q4 and Summer 2025 Q2(b) (2 marks then 3). The first part solves the plain equation and the second begins Hence solve with the angle inside a bracket. Marks run one for isolating the ratio and one for each solution inside the range, with follow-through from the first angle to the second. The front page of the paper asks for 2 decimal places unless the question says otherwise, and an extra angle outside the printed range is penalised.
mustMemorise: Isolate the ratio before touching an inverse function
sin: the partner is 180° − the first angle
cos: the partner is 360° − the first angle
tan: the partner is 180° + the first angle
Keep the minus sign of a negative ratio inside the inverse function
Solve for the bracket first, widening the range to match, then undo in reverse order
Check both answers against the printed range and discard anything outside it
notOnThisSpec: Equations with more than two solutions in the range — FM1-TRG-02 caps it at two
Quadratic trigonometric equations such as 2sin²x − sin x = 0
The sine rule and the cosine rule, which the Teacher Guidance excludes
Radians, and identities such as sin²x + cos²x = 1
Proving or deriving the symmetry rules, rather than reading them off the curve

mustBeAbleTo: Isolate the trigonometric ratio before using an inverse function
Find the first angle with sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹, keeping the sign of a negative ratio
Find the second solution with 180° − a, 360° − a or a + 180°, and say which curve the rule belongs to
Use the CAST diagram, or a sketch of the curve, to place both answers in the right quadrants
Count the solutions a printed range holds by drawing a horizontal line across the curve
Discard every angle outside the printed range, and say plainly when no solution is left
Solve an equation whose angle sits inside a bracket by widening the range first
Undo a bracket in reverse order: the shift before the multiplier

sheet.howExamined: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. A trigonometric equation follows the graph question near the front of every paper read: Summer 2018 Q3(b) (5 marks, a bracket), Summer 2019 Q4(b), Summer 2022 Q4(b) (3 marks then 3), Summer 2023 Q3(b) (3 marks then 3), Summer 2024 Q4, Summer 2025 Q2(b) (2 marks then 3) and Summer 2026 Q4 (2 marks then 3, both over negative ranges). The first part solves the plain equation and the second begins Hence solve with the angle inside a bracket. Marks run one for isolating the ratio and one for each solution inside the range, with follow-through from the first angle to the second. The front page of the paper asks for 2 decimal places unless the question says otherwise, and an extra angle outside the printed range is penalised.
traps: Stopping at the calculator's angle, which is the most reported loss on this topic (Summer 2022 FM1 Q4, Summer 2025 FM1 Q2)
Using another curve's rule for the second angle: 360° − a on a sine, 180° − a on a cosine, or 90° added or taken away on a tangent (Summer 2025 FM1 Q2)
Dropping the minus sign of the ratio before pressing the inverse key (Summer 2018 FM1 Q3, Summer 2019 FM1 Q4, Summer 2023 FM1 Q3)
Taking the inverse function before the ratio has been isolated
Leaving an answer outside the printed range on the answer line (Summer 2019 FM1 Q4)

Undoing a bracket in the wrong order or with the wrong operation: multiplying then adding where the scheme adds then multiplies, or dividing where it multiplies (Summer 2023 FM1 Q3, Summer 2024 FM1 Q4)
Forgetting to widen the range to the one the bracket covers, so a solution is lost at an end
Rounding to fewer than 2 decimal places when the question has not said otherwise

workedExamples.stem: Solve the equation $2\sin x = 1.4$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, giving your answers correct to 2 decimal places.

figure.alt: The graph of y = sin x from 0 to 360 degrees with the line y = 0.7 drawn across it, crossing the curve at 44.43 and 135.57 degrees.

steps.decision: Isolate the ratio before anything else. An inverse sine only makes sense once the equation reads sin x equals a single number, and that number has to lie between -1 and 1.

options: Because $\sin^{-1}$ needs the ratio on its own
Because $1.4$ is too large to be an angle
whyMenu.explain: The inverse function undoes the sine, so it has to act on the sine's own value. Taking $\sin^{-1} 1.4$ asks for an angle that does not exist.

steps.working: Sketch $y = \sin x$ and draw $y = 0.7$ across it. The line cuts the curve $2$ times.
steps.decision: Counting crossings before solving tells you how many answers to produce, so you cannot stop one short. It costs about fifteen seconds.
This is the calculator's angle, always the one in the first quadrant for a positive sine. It is the first crossing on the rising part of the curve.
The arch is symmetrical about $x = 90^\circ$, so the second angle is as far past the mirror as the first is short of it. On the CAST diagram this is the S quadrant.

steps.working: Both $44.43^\circ$ and $135.57^\circ$ lie between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, so both are kept.
steps.decision: The range check is the last line of the working, every time. An angle outside the printed range is not a solution of the question that was asked, and an extra one is penalised.

options.feedback: Both lie between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.
The partner is inside the range too, so it stays on the answer line.
The calculator's angle is inside the range as well; nothing here needs leaving off.

twin.stem: Solve the equation $4\cos x + 3 = 0$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, giving your answers correct to 2 decimal places.

workedExamples.stem:
(a) Solve $\cos x = -0.25$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.
(b) Hence solve $\cos(2x - 40^\circ) = -0.25$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$.
Give every answer correct to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: Part (a) done properly is most of part (b). Keep the minus sign in the calculator, and use cosine's own rule for the partner.

steps.working: As $x$ runs $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$, the bracket runs $-40^\circ$ to $320^\circ$.
steps.decision: Widen the range before you hunt for angles. Doing it the other way round is how solutions get lost, or invented, at the ends.

options: Because the bracket, not $x$, is what the cosine is taken of
Because the range is always doubled
Because the answers must be positive
whyMenu.explain: The equation says something about the bracket. Until the bracket is solved, x has not been touched, so the hunt happens in the bracket's own range.

options.feedback: Double both ends of $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$, then take $40$ away.
That is the range of $x$; the bracket $2x - 40$ covers a different one.
The $40$ was taken away but the ends were not doubled first.

steps.decision: Those are exactly the two angles from part (a), which is what the word "Hence" was promising. Both sit inside the widened range, so neither is discarded.

options.feedback: The bracket takes part (a)'s two angles, both inside its range.
The angles belong to the whole bracket, $2x - 40$, not to $2x$.
Those solve $\cos x = -0.25$; here the bracket, not $x$, takes those values.

steps.decision: Undo in reverse order: the bracket subtracted $40$ last, so add it back first; it multiplied by $2$ first, so divide by it last. Halving before adding gives $92.24^\circ$, which is the reported slip.

steps.working: Both answers lie between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, so both are kept.
steps.decision: Check against the range printed in part (b), not the one in part (a). They are different ranges and only one of them is being asked about.

options.feedback: Both lie between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, the range in part (b).
$147.76^\circ$ is inside $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$ as well.
Part (b) prints its own range, $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$, and both lie inside it.

twin.stem: Solve $\tan x = 2.5$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, giving your answers correct to 2 decimal places.

items.stem:
Three quick checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new work, so answer from what you already know.
Solve $2y = 1.4$.
items.skill: Prerequisite: isolating a quantity in a linear equation

options.feedback: Divide both sides by $2$. The first step of every equation in this topic is exactly this, with $\sin x$ in place of $y$.
That multiplies where it should divide. Undo a multiplication by dividing.
The $2$ has been ignored rather than undone, so the equation is no longer balanced.

items.stem: Which of these numbers is in the range $0^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$?
items.skill: Prerequisite: reading an inequality as a range

options.feedback: The two signs are 'less than or equal to', so the ends count and everything between them does too.
Past $180^\circ$, so outside. A solution outside the printed range earns nothing.
Below $0^\circ$, so outside at the other end. Ranges in this topic are often negative, so read them carefully.

items.stem: On a calculator set to degrees, what is $\tan^{-1} 1.5$, correct to 2 decimal places?
items.skill: Prerequisite: using the inverse tangent key

options.feedback: That is the calculator's angle, the starting point for everything in this lesson.
That is the angle in radians. Set the calculator to degrees first.
That is $90^\circ$ minus the angle, the one whose tangent is $\frac{1}{1.5}$.

items.stem: $\sin^{-1} 0.55 = 33.37^\circ$. What is the other solution of $\sin x = 0.55$ between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$?
items.skill: Find the partner of a sine solution

options.feedback: $180 - 33.37 = 146.63$: the sine arch is symmetrical about $90^\circ$.
$360$ minus the angle is cosine's rule; on the sine curve it lands below the axis.
Adding $180$ is tangent's rule; on the sine curve it flips the sign of the value.

items.stem: $\cos^{-1}(-0.3) = 107.46^\circ$. What is the other solution of $\cos x = -0.3$ between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$?
items.skill: Find the partner of a cosine solution

options.feedback: $360 - 107.46 = 252.54$: the cosine curve is symmetrical about $180^\circ$.
$180$ minus the angle is sine's rule; here it gives the angle for $+0.3$.
Adding $180$ is tangent's rule, and it passes $360^\circ$.

items.stem: $\tan x = 2.2$ has one solution at $65.56^\circ$. Where is the other, between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$?
items.skill: Find the partner of a tangent solution

options.feedback: Tangent repeats every $180^\circ$, so the partner is half a turn on.
$180$ minus the angle is sine's rule; the tangent there is negative.
$360$ minus the angle is cosine's rule; the tangent there is negative too.

items.stem: You are solving $\cos x = -0.55$. What do you type into the calculator?
items.skill: Keeping the sign of the ratio

options.feedback: The minus sign goes in with the number; the angle then lands in the second quarter.

options.text: $\cos^{-1}(0.55)$ and put the minus back later
options.feedback: That gives the angle for $+0.55$, in the wrong quarter; there is no minus to put back afterwards.
That is a negative angle whose cosine is $+0.55$, not $-0.55$.

items.stem: Your two angles for an equation come out as $210^\circ$ and $330^\circ$, and the range printed is $0^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$. What do you write on the answer line?

options.text: Neither: there is no solution in this range
options.feedback: Both angles are past $180^\circ$. Saying so plainly is the answer, and it is worth the mark.

options.text: Both, because the working is correct
options.feedback: An answer outside the printed range is not a solution of the question that was asked, and extra values are penalised.
Smaller is not the same as inside. $210$ is still greater than $180$.

items.skill: Undoing a bracket in reverse order

options.feedback: Take the $15$ away first, then divide by $3$: $90 \div 3 = 30$.
That divides by $3$ before taking the $15$ away; undo the last step first.
That multiplies by $3$ instead of dividing; the bracket already holds $3x$.

items.stem: Which quadrants hold the solutions when $\cos x$ is negative?

options.feedback: **C** sits in the fourth and **A** in the first, so cosine is positive there and negative in the other two: quadrants $2$ and $3$.
Those are the quadrants where sine is positive, which is the A and S pair.
Cosine is positive in the fourth, because that is where the C sits.

items.stem: On a calculator set to degrees, what is $\sin^{-1} 0.5$?
items.skill: Prerequisite: using the inverse sine key

options.feedback: That is the calculator's angle. Everything in this lesson is about the angle it does not offer you.
That is $\sin 0.5^\circ$, the sine of the number rather than the angle with that sine. The inverse key runs the other way.
That is a genuine second solution, and the calculator does not give it. It comes from the curve, which is what the next few screens are about.

items.stem: $\sin^{-1} 0.5 = 30^\circ$. What is the other solution of $\sin x = 0.5$ between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$?
items.skill: Find the partner of a sine solution

options.feedback: $180 - 30 = 150$. The sine arch is symmetrical about $90^\circ$.
$360$ minus the angle is cosine's rule. Here it lands below the axis, where the sine is $-0.5$.
Adding $180$ is tangent's rule. On the sine curve it flips the sign of the value instead of keeping it.

items.stem: $\cos^{-1} -0.5 = 120^\circ$. What is the other solution between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$?
items.skill: Find the partner of a cosine solution

options.feedback: $360 - 120 = 240$. The cosine curve is symmetrical about $180^\circ$.
$180$ minus the angle belongs to sine. Its cosine is $0.5$, which is not what was asked for.
Adding $180$ belongs to tangent. On the cosine curve it changes the sign of the value.

items.stem: $\tan x = 1$ has one solution at $45^\circ$. Where is the other, between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$?
items.skill: Find the partner of a tangent solution

options.feedback: The tangent curve repeats every $180^\circ$, so the partner is simply $180^\circ$ further on.
That is sine's rule, and its tangent is $-1$ rather than $1$.
That is cosine's rule, and its tangent is $-1$.

items.stem: You are solving $\cos x = -0.75$. What do you type into the calculator?
items.skill: Keep the sign of a negative ratio

options.feedback: It returns $138.59^\circ$, which is already in the second quadrant, exactly where a negative cosine belongs.

options.text: $\cos^{-1}(0.75)$ and put the minus back later
options.feedback: That gives $41.41^\circ$, in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive. Both answers then come out in the wrong quadrants.
A minus sign in front of the angle is not the same as a minus sign inside the ratio, and it puts the answer outside a range that starts at zero.

items.skill: Undo a bracket in the right order

options.feedback: Add the $40$ back, then divide by $2$: the reverse of the order the bracket applied them.
That divides first and adds afterwards. The two operations do not commute, so the order is the whole question here.
That multiplies by $2$ where it should divide. The bracket already contains $2x$, so the $2$ has to come off.

context.setting: A sine equation whose answers are whole numbers of degrees

parts.stem:
Solve the equation
$\sin x = 0.5$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °
hints: Start with $\sin^{-1}$ of the number.
Sketch the curve, draw the line across it and count the crossings; there are $2$.
Sine pairs an angle $a$ with $180^\circ - a$. If either lands outside the range, add or take away a full turn of $360^\circ$.
parts.workedSolution:
Isolate the ratio: $\sin x = 0.5$.
The calculator gives $\sin^{-1}(0.5) = 30^\circ$.
Inside the range the solutions are $30$, straight from the calculator and $150$, from $180 - 30$.
Both lie between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, so $x = 30^\circ$ or $x = 150^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one of the two, and it earns its mark. The curve reaches the same height a second time before the range ends: the other solution is $150$, from $180 - 30$.
The first angle is right, so the method marks stand. The second comes from the wrong curve's rule: $360$ minus the angle belongs to cosine, and on this curve it gives a value whose sine is $-0.5$.

questions.solutionProgram: sin x = 0.5 on [0, 360] -> 30, 150; base = 30; wrong-rule route = 330

context.setting: A sine equation with a negative ratio, so both answers are below the axis

parts.stem:
Solve the equation
$\sin x = -0.5$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °
hints: Start with $\sin^{-1}$ of the number.
Sketch the curve, draw the line across it and count the crossings; there are $2$.
Sine pairs an angle $a$ with $180^\circ - a$. If either lands outside the range, add or take away a full turn of $360^\circ$.
parts.workedSolution:
Isolate the ratio: $\sin x = -0.5$.
The calculator gives $\sin^{-1}(-0.5) = -30^\circ$.
Inside the range the solutions are $210$, from $180 - (-30)$ and $330$, from $(-30) + 360$.
Both lie between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, so $x = 210^\circ$ or $x = 330^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one of the two, and it earns its mark. The curve reaches the same height a second time before the range ends: the other solution is $330$, from $(-30) + 360$.
The calculator's $-30^\circ$ is a genuine solution of the equation, and it is outside the range that was printed. Add a full turn to move it in: $-30 + 360 = 330^\circ$.

for $-360^\circ \le x \le 0^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °
hints: Start with $\cos^{-1}$ of the number.

Cosine pairs an angle $a$ with $-a$, which is usually written $360^\circ - a$. If either lands outside the range, add or take away a full turn of $360^\circ$.
parts.workedSolution:
Isolate the ratio: $\cos x = 0.5$.
The calculator gives $\cos^{-1}(0.5) = 60^\circ$.
Inside the range the solutions are $-300$, from $60 - 360$ and $-60$, from $-60$.
Both lie between $-360^\circ$ and $0^\circ$, so $x = -300^\circ$ or $x = -60^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one of the two, and it earns its mark. The curve reaches the same height a second time before the range ends: the other solution is $-60$, from $-60$.

Those are the two solutions in $0^\circ$ to $360^\circ$, and the method behind them is right. The printed range runs the other way, so take a full turn off each: $60 - 360 = -300$ and $300 - 360 = -60$.

parts.stem:
The graph of $y = \sin x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$ is shown above, with the line $y = 0.6$ drawn across it.

Write down how many solutions the equation $5\sin x = 3$ has in this range.

Answer ________

scheme.for: $2$, read as the number of crossings

hints: Divide through first: the equation is the same as $\sin x = 0.6$.
Count where the line meets the curve.
parts.workedSolution: $5\sin x = 3$ is $\sin x = 0.6$, which is the line drawn on the graph. It cuts the curve $2$ times, so there are $2$ solutions.

commonErrors.feedback: The calculator offers one angle, and the picture shows the curve coming back down through the same height before $360^\circ$.

parts.stem:
Solve, correct to 2 decimal places, the equation
$5\sin x = 3$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °
hints: Divide both sides by $5$ first.
The partner of the calculator's angle is $180^\circ$ minus it.
parts.workedSolution:
Divide by $5$: $\sin x = 0.6$.
The calculator gives $\sin^{-1}(0.6) = 36.87^\circ$.
The partner is $180 - 36.87 = 143.13^\circ$.
Both are inside the range, so $x = 36.87^\circ$ or $x = 143.13^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: The division and the first angle are both right, so two of the three marks are safe. Part (a) said how many solutions there are, and the picture above shows the second one waiting past the maximum.
$360$ minus the angle is cosine's rule. On the sine curve that lands below the axis, where $\sin x$ is $-0.6$, not $0.6$.

parts.stem:
Explain how the graph shows that the equation $\sin x = 1.2$ has no solutions for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer ________

accepted: The line y = 1.2 is above the curve, because the greatest value of sin x is 1, so the line never meets the curve and there are no solutions.
sin x can never be more than 1, so a line at 1.2 lies above the graph and never crosses it.

scheme.for: stating that the greatest value of $\sin x$ is $1$
concluding that the line $y = 1.2$ never meets the curve, so there is no solution

hints: Look at how high the curve ever gets.
Then say what a line drawn above that height would do.
parts.workedSolution:
The greatest value of $\sin x$ is $1$, so the whole curve lies on or below the line $y = 1$.
A line drawn at $y = 1.2$ is above the curve everywhere and never crosses it, so the equation has no solutions in the range.

commonErrors.feedback: A calculator error message is a symptom, not a reason. The mark is for saying what the graph shows: the curve never reaches that height.

resources: Scientific calculator
Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

emphasis: hence: the second part uses the first part's angles

context.setting: A cosine equation, then the same ratio inside a bracket

methodLock.requiredMethod: Use the two angles found in part (a) as the values of the bracket, then undo the bracket in reverse order.

parts.stem:
Solve, correct to 2 decimal places, the equation
$\cos x = -0.25$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °

scheme.for: $\cos^{-1}(-0.25)$ attempted with the minus sign kept

hints: Keep the minus sign when you press the inverse cosine.
The cosine curve is symmetrical about $180^\circ$, so the partner is $360^\circ$ minus the first angle.
parts.workedSolution:
The calculator gives $\cos^{-1}(-0.25) = 104.48^\circ$.
The cosine curve is symmetrical about $x = 180^\circ$, so the partner is $360 - 104.48 = 255.52^\circ$.
Both are inside the range, so $x = 104.48^\circ$ or $x = 255.52^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: The calculator's angle is right and earns two of the three marks. The curve dips below that height and comes back up through it before $360^\circ$, so there is a second answer.

parts.stem:
Hence solve, correct to 2 decimal places, the equation
$\cos(2x - 40^\circ) = -0.25$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °

scheme.for: setting the bracket equal to the angles from part (a): $2x - 40 = 104.48$ or $255.52$
adding $40$ to both angles before dividing

hints: The word "Hence" means the two angles from part (a) are the values of the whole bracket.
Work out the range the bracket itself covers: it runs from $-40^\circ$ to $320^\circ$.
Undo the bracket backwards: add the $40$ first, then divide by the $2$.
parts.workedSolution:
As $x$ runs from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$, the bracket $2x - 40$ runs from $-40^\circ$ to $320^\circ$, which holds exactly the two angles from part (a).
So $2x - 40 = 104.48^\circ$ or $255.52^\circ$.
Add $40$: $2x = 144.48^\circ$ or $295.52^\circ$.
Divide by $2$: $x = 72.24^\circ$ or $x = 147.76^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: The two angles are right, so the first method mark stands. The bracket was halved before the $40$ was dealt with. Undo the operations in the reverse of the order they were applied: add first, then divide.
Both values were doubled instead of halved. The bracket already holds $2x$, so the last step divides by $2$; multiplying takes you further away.

resources: Scientific calculator
Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

context.setting: A sine equation with the ratio to isolate first, on numbers of its own

parts.stem:
Solve, correct to 2 decimal places, the equation
$4\sin x = 2.6$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °
hints: Divide by $4$ before you press anything.
Sine pairs an angle $a$ with $180^\circ - a$.
parts.workedSolution:
Isolate the ratio: $\sin x = 0.65$.
The calculator gives $\sin^{-1}(0.65) = 40.54^\circ$.
The partner is $180 - 40.54 = 139.46^\circ$.
Both lie between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, so $x = 40.54^\circ$ or $x = 139.46^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one of the two, and it earns its marks. The sine curve reaches the same height again on the way down, at $180^\circ$ minus this angle.
The first angle is right. The second came from cosine's rule, $360^\circ$ minus the angle, which lands below the axis on the sine curve; sine's partner is $180^\circ$ minus it.

resources: Scientific calculator
Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

context.setting: A cosine equation whose ratio comes out negative

parts.stem:
Solve, correct to 2 decimal places, the equation
$5\cos x + 2 = 0$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °
hints: Take the $2$ away and divide by $5$; keep the minus sign.
Cosine pairs an angle $a$ with $360^\circ - a$.
parts.workedSolution:
Isolate the ratio: $\cos x = -0.4$.
The calculator gives $\cos^{-1}(-0.4) = 113.58^\circ$, in the second quarter.
The partner is $360 - 113.58 = 246.42^\circ$.
Both lie between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, so $x = 113.58^\circ$ or $x = 246.42^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one of the two, and it earns its marks. The cosine curve comes back to the same height the other side of $180^\circ$, at $360^\circ$ minus this angle.
The first angle is right. The second came from sine's rule, $180^\circ$ minus the angle; cosine's partner is $360^\circ$ minus it.
These are the angles for $\cos x = 0.4$: the minus sign was dropped before the inverse key. Typed as $\cos^{-1}(-0.4)$, the angle lands in the second quarter.

resources: Scientific calculator
Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

context.setting: A tangent equation, whose partner is half a turn on

parts.stem:
Solve, correct to 2 decimal places, the equation
$\tan x = 0.8$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °
hints: Tangent repeats every $180^\circ$.
parts.workedSolution:
The calculator gives $\tan^{-1}(0.8) = 38.66^\circ$.
The partner is $38.66 + 180 = 218.66^\circ$.
Both lie between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, so $x = 38.66^\circ$ or $x = 218.66^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one of the two, and it earns its mark. The tangent curve repeats every $180^\circ$, so the same value comes again half a turn on.
The first angle is right. The second came from $360^\circ$ minus the angle, cosine's rule; tangent's partner is the angle plus $180^\circ$.

parts.stem:
Solve, correct to 2 decimal places, the equation
$\sin x = 0.35$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °
hints: Sine pairs an angle $a$ with $180^\circ - a$.
parts.workedSolution:
The calculator gives $\sin^{-1}(0.35) = 20.49^\circ$.
The partner is $180 - 20.49 = 159.51^\circ$.
Both are inside the range, so $x = 20.49^\circ$ or $x = 159.51^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: The calculator's angle is right and earns two of the three marks. The curve comes back to the same height on the way down, at $180^\circ$ minus it.

parts.stem:
Hence solve, correct to 2 decimal places, the equation
$\sin(2x - 20^\circ) = 0.35$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °

scheme.for: setting the bracket equal to the angles from part (a): $2x - 20 = 20.49$ or $159.51$
adding $20$ to both angles before dividing

hints: As $x$ runs from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$, the bracket runs from $-20^\circ$ to $340^\circ$.
Add the $20$ back first, then halve.
parts.workedSolution:
As $x$ runs from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$, the bracket $2x - 20$ runs from $-20^\circ$ to $340^\circ$, which holds exactly the two angles from part (a).
So $2x - 20 = 20.49^\circ$ or $159.51^\circ$.
Add $20$: $2x = 40.49^\circ$ or $179.51^\circ$.
Divide by $2$: $x = 20.24^\circ$ or $x = 89.76^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: The two angles are right, so the first method mark stands. The bracket was halved before the $20$ was added back; undo the last step first, adding $20$, then halve.
Both values were doubled instead of halved. The bracket already holds $2x$, so the last step divides by $2$.

context.setting: A cosine bracket with a shift only, solved without a part to lean on

parts.stem:
Solve, correct to 2 decimal places, the equation
$2\cos(x + 40^\circ) = 1.2$
for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer $x = $ ________ ° , $x = $ ________ °

scheme.for: the bracket's range, $40^\circ$ to $400^\circ$, and both bracket angles in it

hints: Divide by $2$ first.
The bracket $x + 40^\circ$ runs from $40^\circ$ to $400^\circ$.
parts.workedSolution:
Isolate the ratio: $\cos(x + 40^\circ) = 0.6$.
The bracket runs from $40^\circ$ to $400^\circ$; $\cos^{-1}(0.6) = 53.13^\circ$ and $360 - 53.13 = 306.87^\circ$, both inside it.
Take $40$ away: $x = 13.13^\circ$ or $x = 266.87^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: Those are the values of the bracket $x + 40^\circ$, not of $x$. Take the $40$ away to finish.
That is one of the two. The cosine reaches $0.6$ again at $360^\circ$ minus the first bracket angle, which is still inside the bracket's range.

findTheMistake.stem: Sinéad was asked to solve $5\sin x = 3$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, correct to 2 decimal places. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Lines 1 and 2 are right, and they carry two of the three marks: the ratio is isolated and the calculator's angle is correct.
Line 3 uses cosine's rule on a sine equation. Taking the angle from $360^\circ$ reflects it in the x-axis, and $\sin 323.13^\circ = -0.6$, which is the wrong sign as well as the wrong value.
The sine arch is symmetrical about $x = 90^\circ$, so the partner of 36.87$^\circ$ is $180^\circ$ minus it.
correction: Check: sin 143.13 = 0.6, and both angles are inside the range
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks are safe, and the third is one line away. Put the second angle back into the original equation before you write it down: thirty seconds with the calculator would have shown that $323.13^\circ$ gives the wrong sign.

findTheMistake.stem: Cathal was asked to solve $\tan x = 2.5$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, correct to 2 decimal places. His working:
studentWorking: The tangent graph repeats, so there must be more answers
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Line 1 is right and line 2 is the correct thought, which is what makes line 3 such an expensive place to stop.
The tangent curve repeats every $180^\circ$, so $68.20 + 180 = 248.20^\circ$ is also a solution, and it is still inside the range.
The range $0^\circ$ to $360^\circ$ covers two whole branches of the curve, so it holds exactly two answers.
correction: Both lie between 0 and 360, so x = 68.20 or x = 248.20
findTheMistake.feedback: Half the marks, and the second line shows the reasoning was already there. Write the partner down the moment the calculator answers, before the thought goes: for tangent it is always $180^\circ$ more.

findTheMistake.stem: Orlagh was asked to solve $3\sin x + 1 = 0$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, correct to 2 decimal places. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Line 1 is right: the ratio is $-\frac{1}{3}$.
Line 2 drops the minus sign, so every angle after it solves $\sin x = \frac{1}{3}$ instead. A negative sine lives in the third and fourth quarters.
findTheMistake.feedback: Isolating the ratio earned its mark. Type the minus sign into the inverse key with the number; then find both angles below the axis, in the third and fourth quarters.

findTheMistake.stem: Cormac was asked to solve $\tan x = 4.2$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, correct to 2 decimal places. His working:
studentWorking: The tangent graph repeats every 180 degrees
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Lines 1 and 2 are right, and line 2 even says why there is more to find.
Line 3 stops at the calculator's angle. Half a turn on, the tangent repeats, and that angle is still inside the range.
correction: Both lie between 0 and 360, so x = 76.61 or x = 256.61
findTheMistake.feedback: The first angle earns its mark. Every trigonometric equation in a 360-degree range has a partner to find: write it before you write the answer line.

prompts.prompt: Give the four steps for solving a trigonometric equation in a given range.
prompts.answer: Isolate the ratio; take the inverse function for the first angle; use the curve's own rule for the second; then check both against the printed range.

prompts.prompt: Give the rule for the second solution of each of sin x = k, cos x = k and tan x = k.
prompts.answer: For sine, 180 minus the first angle. For cosine, 360 minus it. For tangent, 180 more than it.

prompts.prompt: What do the four letters of the CAST diagram stand for, and what does each one tell you?
prompts.answer: All, Sin, Tan, Cos, read anticlockwise from the first quadrant. Each letter names the ratio that is positive in that quarter turn, so every ratio not named there is negative.

prompts.prompt: Why is the calculator's angle never the whole answer?
prompts.answer: The inverse function returns one angle, and the curve reaches the same height again inside a full turn, so a second solution is waiting in the range.

prompts.prompt: You are solving $\cos x = -0.75$. What must you not do to the minus sign?
prompts.answer: Do not drop it before taking the inverse cosine. Keeping it gives 138.59 degrees straight away, in the second quadrant where a negative cosine belongs.

prompts.prompt: How do you solve an equation whose angle sits inside a bracket, such as $\cos(2x - 40^\circ) = k$?
prompts.answer: Widen the range to the one the bracket covers, solve for the whole bracket, then undo the bracket in reverse order: add the 40 back first, divide by the 2 second.

prompts.prompt: What is the last line of working on every question in this topic?
prompts.answer: The range check: both answers written out and compared with the range printed in the question, with anything outside it discarded.

prompts.prompt: Which rule gives the second solution of $\sin x = k$?
An angle sits inside a bracket. What do you widen first?
prompts.answer: The range, to the one the bracket covers.

findings.asked: Solve a trig equation in a range.
findings.wentWrong: First-part wrong answers (60 and 300) were common; the CAST diagram with a negative value caused difficulty; algebra to isolate x undid correct values.
findings.rule: Solve for the bracket first, find all angles from CAST, then isolate x.

findings.asked: Solve a trig equation with a negative value; give solutions in range.
findings.wentWrong: 0.184 used instead of -0.184; both angles from (i) were followed through into (ii) giving a solution outside the range.
findings.rule: Check every candidate solution against the stated range.

findings.asked: Solve a trig equation in a given range.
findings.wentWrong: Most found the basic angle (53.13) and stopped; the sketch from part (a) was not used to locate the other angles; part (ii) follow-through only.
findings.rule: Use the sketch to see how many solutions the range contains.

findings.wentWrong: Some used cos inverse of 2/3 and got plus or minus 48.19 with the wrong sign; in (ii) dividing by 2 instead of multiplying.
findings.rule: Keep the sign of the ratio and undo the bracket in the correct order.

findings.asked: Solve a trig equation with a transformed argument.
findings.wentWrong: The second angle was found by most; the common slip was multiplying by 2 and then adding 20 instead of the reverse order.
findings.rule: If the argument is (2x + 20), subtract 20 first, then divide by 2.

findings.asked: Solve tan x = 6 in a range, then use it.
findings.wentWrong: tan inverse gave 80.54 and many stopped; some added or subtracted from 90 and left the range; follow-through was available in (ii).
findings.rule: For tan, the second solution is 180 more.

insight.ruleToRemember: Find the basic angle, use CAST or the sketch to list every solution of the bracket in the range, then undo the bracket in reverse order; discard anything outside the range.
insight.aStarSignal: A negative ratio with a transformed argument, solved with every solution in range and none outside it.

checks.detail: Every solution comes from solutionsIn in scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/lib.mjs, which scans the principal angles, and every one is substituted back through Math.sin, Math.cos or Math.tan and checked against its range before it is printed. Exact cases: sin x = 0.5 on [0, 360] -> 30, 150; cos x = -0.5 on [0, 360] -> 120, 240; tan x = 1 on [0, 360] -> 45, 225; sin x = -0.5 on [0, 360] -> 210, 330; cos x = 0.5 on [-360, 0] -> -300, -60; tan x = -1 on [0, 360] -> 135, 315. Decimal cases to 2 d.p.: sin x = 0.7 -> 44.43, 135.57; cos x = -0.75 -> 138.59, 221.41; tan x = 2.5 -> 68.20, 248.20; sin x = 0.6 -> 36.87, 143.13; cos x = -0.25 -> 104.48, 255.52. Bracket case: cos(2x - 40) = -0.25 on [0, 180] widens to [-40, 320], inner angles 104.48, 255.52, so x = 72.24, 147.76. Rounding was checked both ways round: rounding the first angle and then applying the rule gives the same 2 d.p. value as applying the rule and rounding afterwards, for every case above. Distractors come from baseAngleOnly, wrongSecondSolution, signOfRatioDropped, shiftAfterDividing and transformOrderSwapped in scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/routes.mjs, never typed by hand, and verify-published.mjs re-executes each one against the published JSON.

checks.tool: claude (FM1 batch-C generator scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/gen-trig-equations.mjs; every solution set produced by solutionsIn over the principal angles, every route re-executed against the published JSON by verify-published.mjs and every part fed to the app's own marker by check-marking.mts)
checks.detail: Solution sets are encoded as the brief requires: kind algebraic, latex "x=30, x=150" in the question's own letter, equivalence equivalent, variables ["x"]. Fed through src/components/items/mark.ts the engine accepts every natural spelling — "30, 150", "x=30 or x=150", the two values in either order and braces round them — and reports a single value as a partial solution set, which is exactly the feedback this topic needs. One spelling it does not parse is a degree symbol typed after each number, so every such part prints the degree sign on its answer line and carries a text common error that recognises that spelling and awards the part's marks in full with one line about the format.

checks.detail: Every solution comes from solutionsIn in scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/lib.mjs, which scans the principal angles, and every one is substituted back through Math.sin, Math.cos or Math.tan and checked against its range before it is printed. Exact cases: sin x = 0.5 on [0, 360] -> 30, 150; cos x = -0.5 on [0, 360] -> 120, 240; tan x = 1 on [0, 360] -> 45, 225; sin x = -0.5 on [0, 360] -> 210, 330; cos x = 0.5 on [-360, 0] -> -300, -60; tan x = -1 on [0, 360] -> 135, 315. Decimal cases to 2 d.p.: sin x = 0.7 -> 44.43, 135.57; cos x = -0.75 -> 138.59, 221.41; tan x = 2.5 -> 68.20, 248.20; sin x = 0.6 -> 36.87, 143.13; cos x = -0.25 -> 104.48, 255.52. Bracket case: cos(2x - 40) = -0.25 on [0, 180] widens to [-40, 320], inner angles 104.48, 255.52, so x = 72.24, 147.76. Rounding was checked both ways round: rounding the first angle and then applying the rule gives the same 2 d.p. value as applying the rule and rounding afterwards, for every case above. Distractors come from baseAngleOnly, wrongSecondSolution, signOfRatioDropped, shiftAfterDividing and transformOrderSwapped in scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/routes.mjs, never typed by hand, and verify-published.mjs re-executes each one against the published JSON.

checks.detail: Solution sets are encoded as the brief requires: kind algebraic, latex "x=30, x=150" in the question's own letter, equivalence equivalent, variables ["x"].
